meta.title: Cosmic History Emaki
meta.tagline: We study history in order to learn from it
meta.hint: Wheel / pinch to zoom · drag to move · tap a card or person for details · Note: the time axis is compressed for each era

future.name: Future
future.catch: Now it is your turn to learn from history and shape the age.

bang.name: Birth of the Universe
bang.summary: About 13.8 billion years ago, the universe began from a hot, dense state. The first 380,000 years are shown with the time axis heavily compressed.
features: The beginning of all matter and space
Rapid expansion (inflation) in a very short time
In about three minutes, nuclei of hydrogen and helium form
About 380,000 years later, light can travel straight

dark.name: The First Stars
dark.summary: After a dark age, the first stars and galaxies began to light up.
dark.catch: The first light kindles in the darkness
features: A "dark age" with neither stars nor galaxies continues
The first stars are born
The first galaxies form and the universe is reionized
Recent space telescopes have found galaxies from this era

galaxy.name: Age of Galaxies
galaxy.summary: Galaxies grow, and heavy elements are made inside stars. The universe's expansion eventually turns to acceleration.
features: Repeated birth and death of stars makes carbon, oxygen and iron
The Milky Way grows
There was a peak period of star formation
Expansion accelerates and dark energy comes to dominate

solar.name: The Solar System and Earth
solar.summary: 4.6 billion years ago, the solar system was born from a cloud of gas and dust, and Earth and the Moon formed.
features: The Sun and planets are born from the same cloud
Earth cools from a scorching state
The Moon is said to have formed in a giant impact
There is evidence that oceans formed early

life.name: Origin of Life
life.summary: Life arose in the sea, photosynthesis changed the atmosphere, and cells grew more complex.
features: The oldest traces of life are about 3.5–3.8 billion years old
Photosynthesis raises oxygen in the atmosphere
Cells with a nucleus (eukaryotes) appear
After snowball Earth, large organisms emerge

paleo.name: Paleozoic Era
paleo.summary: The forms of living things diversified at once, and life spread from the sea onto land. The era ends with the greatest mass extinction in history.
paleo.catch: From sea to land, life advances
features: The Cambrian explosion brings out the basic animal body plans
Fishes, plants and insects appear
Vertebrates come ashore
At the end of the Permian, the greatest mass extinction occurs

meso.name: Mesozoic Era
meso.summary: The age of the dinosaurs. The ancestors of mammals and birds appeared, and flowers bloomed. It closes with a giant asteroid impact.
features: Dinosaurs flourish
Small mammals live in their shadow
Birds and flowering plants appear
A giant asteroid impact drives the dinosaurs extinct

ceno.name: Age of Mammals
ceno.summary: With the dinosaurs gone, mammals diversified and the line from primates to apes took shape.
ceno.catch: When our ancestors lived in the trees
features: Mammals diversify all at once
Primates, and later apes, appear
The rise of the Himalayas and cooling change the climate
Grasslands spread and animals come down from the forests

hominin.name: Birth of Humankind
hominin.summary: Splitting from the common ancestor with chimpanzees, humans move toward upright walking, stone tools and the use of fire. A long human journey begins.
hominin.catch: They began to walk on two feet
features: Upright walking begins
The oldest stone tools
The genus Homo appears and spreads out of Africa
With fire, brains grow larger

sapiens.name: Homo sapiens
sapiens.summary: About 300,000 years ago, we appeared in Africa. Spreading worldwide, we survived the ice ages with language, art and tools.
sapiens.catch: The origin story of our species
features: Born in Africa and spread across the world
The birth of symbols and art, such as cave paintings
Meeting Neanderthals and others, then becoming the only humans
Crossing the ice age and reaching the Americas too

civ.name: Farming and Civilization
civ.summary: Farming and herding began, and settlements, cities, writing and states arose.
features: The start of farming and herding
Cities and the invention of writing
The civilizations of Egypt, Mesopotamia, the Indus and China
From bronze to iron

ancient.name: Antiquity and the Middle Ages
ancient.summary: People looked up at the stars and began to think about the shape of the universe. A long age of thought on whether Earth is a sphere and where the world's center is.
ancient.catch: People saw order in the night sky
features: Ancient Greece begins to reason about the universe
Earth is found to be a sphere whose size can be measured
The geocentric model long remains the accepted view
Observation and calculation develop in the Islamic world and elsewhere

revolution.name: Scientific Revolution
revolution.summary: Heliocentrism, the telescope, universal gravitation. The universe came to be seen as explainable by laws, not myth.
revolution.catch: Earth was not the center of the universe
features: The rise of heliocentrism
Direct observation of celestial bodies by telescope
Newton explains heaven and earth by the same law
Evolution and electromagnetism change the way we see the world

modern.name: Modern Physics
modern.summary: Relativity and quantum theory appeared, and the universe was found to be expanding and to have a beginning. Ideas of black holes and the holographic principle also arise.
features: Relativity changes how we see time and space
The discovery of cosmic expansion and Big Bang theory
Black holes, dark matter and inflation
Toward the holographic principle linking information and gravity

now.name: Today's View of the Universe
now.summary: Detection of gravitational waves, imaging of a black hole, the Webb telescope. Our picture of the universe is still being updated.
now.catch: The universe is still being checked against the answers
features: About 5% of the universe's makeup is ordinary matter
Gravitational waves and black holes are caught directly
The Webb telescope sees the earliest universe
The nature of dark matter and dark energy is still a mystery
Debates over the interpretation of quantum theory, such as the measurement problem and many-worlds, continue

near.name: The Near Future
near.summary: The universe over the next several thousand years. Astronomical phenomena that are certain to occur stand beside futures that humanity will choose.
near.catch: The future is already half decided
features: Cyclical events such as eclipses and comets can be predicted
Beyond here lies the realm of "prediction" and "hypothesis"
Humanity's choices can change Earth's future

far.name: The Far Future
far.summary: Tens of thousands to billions of years from now. Ice ages, galaxy collisions, the aging of the Sun. All are predictions based on current science.
far.catch: Even the Sun has a lifespan
features: Predictions may change as research advances
The Sun gradually brightens and changes Earth's environment
In about 5 billion years, the Sun becomes a red giant

end.name: The Universe's End
end.summary: Tens of billions to hundreds of trillions of years from now. A far-future picture, debated, in which star birth stops and the last star fades.
end.catch: Until the last star goes out
features: Cosmic expansion accelerates and distant galaxies become invisible
Star birth eventually ends
What lies further beyond is still unsettled

c001.title: Big Bang
c001.detail: The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense state and started to expand.
c001.lesson: The beginning was a state in which everything in today's universe was compressed.
c001.label: About 13.8 billion years ago

c002.title: Inflation
c002.detail: A theory that the universe expanded explosively right after its birth. The fluctuations that seeded later structure are thought to have arisen then.
c002.label: Just after birth (theory)

c003.title: Particle Soup
c003.detail: Elementary particles such as quarks and gluons flew about, and protons and neutrons soon formed.
c003.lesson: The ingredients of matter were assembled almost at once.
c003.label: About 1 second after birth (compressed)

c004.title: Nucleosynthesis
c004.detail: About three minutes after birth, nuclei of hydrogen, helium and others formed. Most of the universe's elements are still hydrogen and helium.
c004.lesson: The light elements were settled in the first three minutes.
c004.label: About 3 minutes after birth (compressed)

c005.title: Recombination
c005.detail: About 380,000 years later, electrons joined nuclei and light could travel freely. That light is still observed as the cosmic microwave background.
c005.lesson: The oldest light still reaches us today.
c005.label: About 380,000 years later

c006.title: Dark Ages
c006.detail: After recombination, a dark era lasted hundreds of millions of years until stars and galaxies formed.
c006.lesson: Even in the lightless era, gravity was slowly gathering matter.
c006.label: Until about 100 million years later

c007.title: First Stars
c007.detail: The first stars (Population III), made of only hydrogen and helium, were born and light returned to the universe.
c007.lesson: The first light in the universe came from a very few giant stars.
c007.label: About 150 million years later

c008.title: Earliest Galaxies
c008.detail: Observations such as those by the Webb telescope have found galaxies only about 300 million years after the Big Bang.
c008.lesson: Looking far is looking into the past.
c008.label: About 300 million years later

c009.title: Reionization
c009.detail: Light from stars and galaxies ionized the hydrogen gas filling the universe again, over hundreds of millions to a billion years.
c009.lesson: The first stars rewrote the shape of the universe.
c009.label: About 200 million–1 billion years later

c010.title: Proto–Milky Way
c010.detail: The clusters of stars that would become our Milky Way began to form.
c010.lesson: Our galaxy, too, grew from small gatherings.
c010.label: About 13 billion years ago

c011.title: Heavier Elements Increase
c011.detail: Fusion inside stars and supernova explosions made heavier elements such as carbon, oxygen and iron, scattering them into space. They became the material of later planets and life.
c011.lesson: Our bodies were once inside stars.
c011.label: Generations of stars

c012.title: Peak of Star Formation
c012.detail: The period when stars formed most actively in the universe, called "cosmic noon."
c012.lesson: The universe, too, had its busy prime.
c012.label: About 10 billion years ago

c013.title: Expansion Accelerates
c013.detail: The influence of dark energy grew, and the expansion of the universe is thought to have begun accelerating.
c013.lesson: The fate of the universe depends on an unseen force.
c013.label: About 6–5 billion years ago

c014.title: Birth of the Solar System
c014.detail: A cloud of gas and dust collapsed, forming the prototypes of the Sun and planets.
c014.lesson: Our place was an unremarkable corner of a galaxy.
c014.label: About 4.6 billion years ago

c015.title: Birth of Earth
c015.detail: Planetesimals gathered and Earth took shape.
c015.lesson: At birth, Earth was a ball of fire.
c015.label: About 4.54 billion years ago

c016.title: Birth of the Moon
c016.detail: A body is thought to have struck the young Earth, and the Moon formed from the debris (the Giant Impact hypothesis).
c016.lesson: The Moon is Earth's companion, and a memory of a collision.
c016.label: About 4.5 billion years ago

c017.title: Birth of the Oceans
c017.detail: Earth cooled, water vapor fell as rain, and oceans formed. Minerals about 4.4 billion years old hold traces of liquid water.
c017.lesson: The stage for life was prepared early.
c017.label: About 4.4 billion years ago

c018.title: Origin of Life
c018.detail: The first life arose in the sea. Fossil and chemical traces go back about 3.5–3.8 billion years.
c018.lesson: Life began soon after Earth cooled.
c018.label: About 3.8–3.5 billion years ago

c019.title: Dawn of Photosynthesis
c019.detail: Cyanobacteria began photosynthesis and released oxygen.
c019.lesson: Tiny organisms changed the planet's environment.
c019.label: About 2.7 billion years ago

c020.title: Great Oxidation Event
c020.detail: Atmospheric oxygen rose, a crisis for many anaerobic organisms but opening the way to organisms that use oxygen.
c020.lesson: Organisms that change their environment change themselves.
c020.label: About 2.4 billion years ago

c021.title: Rise of Eukaryotes
c021.detail: Cells with a nucleus (eukaryotes) appeared. Mitochondria are thought to originate from engulfed bacteria.
c021.label: About 2 billion years ago

c022.title: Multicellular Life
c022.detail: Multicellular organisms, in which cells join to form one body, appeared in various lineages.
c022.label: About 1 billion years ago

c023.title: Snowball Earth
c023.detail: The whole Earth is thought to have frozen over (the Snowball Earth hypothesis). Warming and larger organisms followed.
c023.label: About 700 million years ago

c024.title: Ediacaran Biota
c024.detail: Large, soft-bodied organisms appeared in the sea.
c024.lesson: Life had begun to grow large even before the Cambrian explosion.
c024.label: About 570 million years ago

c025.title: Cambrian Explosion
c025.detail: From about 540 million years ago, the major animal groups appeared within a short span.
c025.label: About 540 million years ago

c026.title: Rise of Fishes
c026.detail: Vertebrates, animals with backbones, began to flourish in the sea.
c026.lesson: The roots of our backbone lie in the sea.
c026.label: About 500 million years ago

c027.title: Land Plants
c027.detail: Plants moved onto land and greatly changed the terrestrial environment.
c027.lesson: Plants opened up the land first.
c027.label: About 470 million years ago

c028.title: Insects and Forests
c028.detail: Insects appeared and forests began to spread across land.
c028.lesson: Land ecosystems were built around forests.
c028.label: About 400 million years ago

c029.title: Vertebrates Move onto Land
c029.detail: Fossils such as Tiktaalik show the transition from fish to four-legged animals.
c029.lesson: The ancestors of legs were fins.
c029.label: About 370 million years ago

c030.title: Carboniferous Forests
c030.detail: Forests of giant ferns spread and later became coal.
c030.label: About 300 million years ago

c031.title: Greatest Mass Extinction
c031.detail: At the end of the Permian, around 90% of marine species are thought to have died out, mainly due to huge volcanic activity.
c031.lesson: Great extinctions also heralded later flourishing.
c031.label: About 250 million years ago

c032.title: Rise of the Dinosaurs
c032.detail: Dinosaurs appeared and eventually became the dominant land animals.
c032.lesson: The leading role is not eternal.
c032.label: About 230 million years ago

c033.title: Ancestors of Mammals
c033.detail: Small ancestors of mammals appeared. Throughout the dinosaur age they lived in ways such as being nocturnal.
c033.lesson: Small beings prepare for later ages.
c033.label: About 220 million years ago

c034.title: Ancestors of Birds
c034.detail: Birds evolved from feathered dinosaurs. Fossils of Archaeopteryx are known.
c034.label: About 150 million years ago

c035.title: Flowers Appear
c035.detail: Flowering plants appeared and diversified through coevolution with insects.
c035.label: About 130 million years ago

c036.title: Extinction of the Dinosaurs
c036.detail: A giant asteroid impact abruptly changed the climate, and non-avian dinosaurs and others died out.
c036.lesson: A single moment can end an era.
c036.label: About 66 million years ago

c037.title: Mammals Diversify
c037.detail: Mammals spread into the vacated ecosystems and branched into many forms.
c037.lesson: An empty seat calls for a new lead.
c037.label: About 60 million years ago

c038.title: Rise of Primates
c038.lesson: Grasping with hands nurtured the brain.
c038.label: About 55 million years ago

c039.title: Rise of the Himalayas
c039.detail: The Indian subcontinent collided with Eurasia and the Himalayas began to rise.
c039.label: About 50 million years ago

c040.title: Cooling and Ice Sheets
c040.detail: Ice sheets spread across Antarctica and Earth moved toward a cooler climate.
c040.lesson: Climate changes with the arrangement of the land.
c040.label: About 34 million years ago

c041.title: Rise of the Apes
c041.detail: Lineages of tailless apes appeared, later leading to humans.
c041.lesson: Humans are one of the apes.
c041.label: About 25 million years ago

c042.title: Spread of Grasslands
c042.detail: Drying spread grasslands, affecting primates that came to live away from forests.
c042.lesson: Environmental change changes the stage of evolution.
c042.label: About 10 million years ago

c043.title: Birth of Humankind
c043.detail: The oldest human fossils that split from the common ancestor with chimpanzees have been found (e.g. Sahelanthropus).
c043.lesson: Our lineage has traveled about seven million years.
c043.label: About 7 million years ago

c044.title: Upright Walking
c044.detail: Evidence of upright walking has been found, e.g. in Ardipithecus.
c044.lesson: Freed hands opened the door to tools.
c044.label: About 4.4 million years ago

c045.title: Oldest Stone Tools
c045.detail: Stone tools about 3.3 million years old have been found in Kenya.
c045.lesson: Tools began before the human brain grew.
c045.label: About 3.3 million years ago

c046.title: Lucy
c046.detail: The fossil "Lucy," of Australopithecus afarensis, was an important clue to upright walking.
c046.lesson: A single fossil can rewrite human history.
c046.label: About 3.2 million years ago

c047.title: Genus Homo Appears
c047.detail: The genus Homo, such as Homo habilis, appeared.
c047.lesson: The definition of "human" changes bit by bit.
c047.label: About 2.4 million years ago

c048.title: Homo erectus
c048.detail: Homo erectus, large-bodied and able to walk long distances, appeared and later spread out of Africa.
c048.lesson: The power to go far widened human history.
c048.label: About 1.9 million years ago

c049.title: Use of Fire
c049.detail: Evidence of fire use goes back about a million years. Cooking is thought to have contributed to brain growth.
c049.lesson: Fire was humanity's first energy revolution.
c049.label: From about 1 million years ago

c050.title: Neanderthals
c050.detail: A close relative of Homo sapiens that lived in Europe and western Asia. Disappeared about 40,000 years ago.
c050.lesson: Other humans once shared this Earth.
c050.label: About 400,000 years ago

c051.title: Birth of Homo sapiens
c051.detail: We, Homo sapiens, appeared in Africa. Sites such as Jebel Irhoud in Morocco are among the oldest evidence.
c051.lesson: Our species' history is about 300,000 years.
c051.label: About 300,000 years ago

c052.title: Out of Africa
c052.detail: Homo sapiens began spreading beyond Africa. Genetic studies suggest a major dispersal about 70,000–60,000 years ago.
c052.lesson: The journey went on out of curiosity.
c052.label: About 70,000–60,000 years ago

c053.title: Language and Symbols
c053.detail: Cultures using symbols, such as language, ornament and ritual, spread across regions.
c053.lesson: The power to share stories enlarged groups.
c053.label: From about 50,000 years ago

c054.title: Cave Paintings
c054.detail: Wall paintings about 45,000 years old have been found in a cave in Indonesia.
c054.lesson: People drew and left what they saw.
c054.label: About 45,000 years ago

c055.title: Neanderthal Extinction
c055.detail: By about 40,000 years ago, Neanderthals had vanished. A little of their DNA remains in Homo sapiens.
c055.lesson: Though we parted, our genes had mixed.
c055.label: About 40,000 years ago

c056.title: To the Japanese Archipelago
c056.detail: There is evidence that humans reached the Japanese archipelago (Upper Paleolithic).
c056.lesson: Japan's history is also part of this journey.
c056.label: About 38,000 years ago

c057.title: Last Glacial Maximum
c057.detail: The coldest period on Earth. Sea levels dropped greatly and land bridges appeared.
c057.lesson: The Ice Age made paths for human migration.
c057.label: About 20,000 years ago

c058.title: Into the Americas
c058.detail: Humans reached the Americas. The timing is debated.
c058.lesson: Humans walked to the ends of the Earth.
c058.label: About 15,000 years ago

c059.title: End of the Ice Age
c059.detail: The last ice age ended and the warm era leading to the present (the Holocene) began.
c059.lesson: A stable climate was a precondition for farming.
c059.label: About 11,700 years ago

c060.title: Dawn of Agriculture
c060.detail: Farming and herding began in places such as western Asia.
c060.label: About 10,000 years ago

c061.title: Göbekli Tepe
c061.detail: Ruins of a huge stone temple in Turkey, among the world's oldest. It shows people gathered even before farming.
c061.lesson: Belief became a reason to gather.
c061.label: From about 11,500 years ago

c062.title: The First Cities
c062.detail: Cities with concentrated populations arose, as at Uruk in Mesopotamia.
c062.lesson: Cities became places of specialization and record-keeping.
c062.label: Around 3500 BCE

c063.title: Invention of Writing
c063.detail: Writing was invented, as cuneiform in Mesopotamia and hieroglyphs in Egypt.
c063.label: Around 3200 BCE

c064.title: Great Pyramid
c064.detail: The Great Pyramid of Giza, Egypt, was built.
c064.lesson: A huge structure is proof of a huge organization.
c064.label: Around 2560 BCE

c065.title: Iron Age
c065.lesson: The material of tools gave the age its name.
c065.label: Around 1200 BCE

c066.title: A Spherical Earth
c066.detail: Greek scholars concluded Earth is round, based on evidence such as the round shadow in lunar eclipses.
c066.lesson: Observation and reasoning identified a shape that couldn't be seen.
c066.label: 5th century BCE

c067.title: The Geocentric Model
c067.detail: Aristotle systematized a cosmos with the celestial bodies revolving around Earth.
c067.lesson: Common sense comes from the most systematic explanation.
c067.label: 4th century BCE

c068.title: Sun-Centered Idea
c068.detail: Aristarchus proposed that Earth revolves around the Sun.
c068.lesson: Even a correct idea may be ahead of its time.
c068.label: 3rd century BCE

c069.title: Size of the Earth
c069.detail: Eratosthenes calculated Earth's size from the difference in the Sun's angle at two places.
c069.lesson: Measuring lets us know the unseen.
c069.label: 3rd century BCE

c070.title: Almagest
c070.detail: Ptolemy organized the geocentric model mathematically. It was used for over 1,000 years as a system explaining the complex motions of the planets.
c070.lesson: A well-made theory survives a long time.
c070.label: 2nd century

c071.title: Islamic Astronomy
c071.detail: In the Islamic world, observation and calculation developed, inheriting and refining Greek knowledge.
c071.label: 9th–15th centuries

c072.title: Supernova Records
c072.detail: In China, Japan and elsewhere, suddenly appearing bright stars (supernovae) were recorded. One became the later Crab Nebula.
c072.lesson: Records help research a thousand years later.

c073.title: Movable-Type Printing
c073.detail: Gutenberg's printing changed the speed at which knowledge spread.
c073.lesson: The circulation of information accelerates science.
c073.label: Mid-15th century

c074.title: Heliocentrism
c074.detail: Copernicus presented a Sun-centered cosmos in On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres.
c074.lesson: Doubting common sense became the starting point of science.

c075.title: Kepler's Laws
c075.detail: Kepler showed that planets move in elliptical orbits, among other laws.

c076.title: Galileo's Telescope
c076.detail: Galileo observed Jupiter's moons and more through a telescope and gained evidence supporting heliocentrism.
c076.lesson: The power of confirming with your own eyes.

c077.title: Universal Gravitation
c077.detail: In the Principia, Newton showed that an apple and the Moon obey the same gravity.
c077.lesson: Heaven and Earth moved by the same law.

c078.title: Nebular Hypothesis
c078.detail: Kant and Laplace proposed that the solar system was born from a cloud of gas.
c078.lesson: The idea that the universe too has a history.

c079.title: Age of the Earth
c079.detail: Hutton held that rock strata form over long spans of time (a forerunner of uniformitarianism).
c079.lesson: Widening the scale of time advances science.

c080.title: Discovery of Neptune
c080.detail: From irregularities in Uranus's motion, Neptune's position was predicted by calculation and then found.
c080.lesson: Theory found a body no one could see.

c081.title: Theory of Evolution
c081.detail: Darwin presented evolution by natural selection in On the Origin of Species.

c082.title: Electromagnetism
c082.detail: Maxwell compiled equations unifying electricity, magnetism and light. Light was found to be an electromagnetic wave.
c082.lesson: Separate things were in fact the same.

c083.title: Quantum Hypothesis
c083.detail: Planck proposed the quantum idea that energy takes only discrete values.
c083.lesson: The small world differs from intuition.

c084.title: Special Relativity
c084.detail: From the constancy of the speed of light, Einstein showed that time and space vary with the observer. E=mc² follows from it.

c085.title: General Relativity
c085.detail: Einstein showed that gravity is the curvature of spacetime. It became the basis for later theories of black holes and cosmic expansion.
c085.lesson: Gravity was not a force but a shape.

c086.title: Verified by an Eclipse
c086.detail: Observations of a total solar eclipse measured starlight bending near the Sun, supporting general relativity.

c087.title: Galaxies Beyond the Milky Way
c087.detail: Hubble showed that the Andromeda Nebula is another galaxy outside the Milky Way.
c087.lesson: The universe was far larger than thought.

c088.title: The Expanding Universe
c088.detail: Lemaître derived from general relativity that the universe is expanding. In 1931 he proposed that it began from the explosion of a "primeval atom."
c088.lesson: Theory pointed to the shape of the universe first.

c089.title: Hubble's Law
c089.detail: Hubble showed by observation that more distant galaxies recede faster.

c090.title: Hints of Dark Matter
c090.detail: Zwicky pointed out from the motion of galaxy clusters that unseen mass is needed. Rubin's later observations made it more convincing.
c090.lesson: The unseen was most of the universe's mass.

c091.title: Big Bang Theory
c091.detail: Gamow and colleagues proposed that the universe began as a hot fireball from which elements formed. The cosmic background radiation was also predicted.

c092.title: Artificial Satellite
c092.detail: Sputnik 1 was launched and humanity went out into space.
c092.lesson: Space turned from something to look at into a place to go.

c093.title: Humans in Space
c093.detail: Gagarin became the first human to fly in space.

c094.title: Cosmic Background Radiation
c094.detail: Penzias and Wilson accidentally discovered radio waves arriving from the whole sky, which proved to be evidence of the Big Bang.
c094.lesson: Accidental noise was the universe's first cry.

c095.title: Apollo 11
c095.detail: Humans stepped onto the Moon's surface.
c095.lesson: Space became a place within reach.

c096.title: Evidence for Dark Matter
c096.detail: Rubin showed unseen mass exists from observations of galaxy rotation speeds.

c097.title: Black Hole Thermodynamics
c097.detail: Bekenstein proposed that black holes have entropy proportional to their surface area. It became the starting point of the later holographic principle.
c097.lesson: Does information dwell in surface area?

c098.title: Hawking Radiation
c098.detail: Hawking showed that black holes emit light through quantum effects and slowly evaporate.
c098.lesson: Even black holes are not eternal.

c099.title: Information Paradox
c099.detail: The question was raised of what happens to information that fell in when a black hole evaporates. Still an important research topic.

c100.title: Inflation Theory
c100.detail: Guth proposed the idea of explosive expansion right after birth. It can explain the flatness of the universe and more.

c101.title: Hubble Space Telescope
c101.detail: The Hubble Space Telescope was launched, allowing the universe to be observed sharply.

c102.title: Ripples in the Background Radiation
c102.detail: The COBE satellite detected tiny temperature fluctuations in the cosmic background radiation, showing the "seeds" of galaxies.
c102.lesson: Slight ripples were the seeds of galaxies.

c103.title: Holographic Principle
c103.detail: 't Hooft proposed that the information of a three-dimensional space including gravity can be described on its two-dimensional boundary, and Susskind developed it.
c103.lesson: The world's information may lie on its boundary.

c104.title: Exoplanets
c104.detail: The first planet orbiting a star other than the Sun was discovered.

c105.title: AdS/CFT Correspondence
c105.detail: Maldacena proposed a correspondence in which a theory of gravity is equivalent to a quantum theory on its boundary. Widely studied as a concrete realization of the holographic principle.
c105.lesson: Gravity may be another face of a different theory.

c106.title: Discovery of Accelerating Expansion
c106.detail: Observations of distant supernovae showed the universe's expansion is accelerating, suggesting dark energy.

c107.title: Bohr's Atomic Model
c107.detail: Bohr presented an atomic model in which electrons can exist only in discrete orbits.
c107.lesson: Classical common sense broke down in the atomic world.

c108.title: Kaluza–Klein Theory
c108.detail: Kaluza and Klein showed that gravity and electromagnetism could be unified in five-dimensional spacetime, with the unseen extra dimension curled up small. It was the origin of the idea of extra dimensions.
c108.lesson: Unseen dimensions may unify the forces.

c109.title: Matrix Mechanics
c109.detail: Heisenberg and others built quantum mechanics describing the atomic world using only observable quantities.
c109.lesson: Build theory only from what can be seen.

c110.title: The Wave Function
c110.detail: Schrödinger gave an equation expressing a particle's state by the wave function ψ. Born interpreted its squared magnitude as the probability of finding the particle.
c110.lesson: The world was described as a wave of probability.

c111.title: Uncertainty Principle
c111.detail: Heisenberg showed that position and momentum cannot both be determined precisely.
c111.lesson: Even the act of measuring has limits.

c112.title: The Measurement Problem and the Copenhagen Interpretation
c112.detail: Bohr and others held that measurement "collapses" the wave function to one result. But the measurement problem — what is observation, and when does collapse occur — remained, and debate continues.
c112.lesson: What observation is became one of physics' biggest questions.

c113.title: Schrödinger's Cat
c113.detail: Schrödinger offered a thought experiment showing that applying superposition to everyday-sized objects leads to absurdity.
c113.lesson: Questions that expose a theory's limits sharpen the theory.

c114.title: EPR Paradox
c114.detail: Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen asked whether quantum mechanics is incomplete. The "entanglement" tying distant particles was later actually confirmed.
c114.lesson: "Spooky action at a distance" was real.

c115.title: Many-Worlds Interpretation
c115.detail: Everett proposed that the wave function does not collapse and that every outcome of each observation is realized in separate worlds.
c115.lesson: The idea that observation does not settle on a single result.

c116.title: Bell's Inequality
c116.detail: Bell showed quantum predictions that local hidden variables cannot explain, in a form testable by experiment.
c116.lesson: A philosophical dispute became something experiment could settle.

c117.title: Birth of String Theory
c117.detail: Veneziano found a formula describing particle scattering, and Nambu and others later interpreted particles as vibrating "strings."
c117.lesson: Not points but strings may be the stuff of the world.

c118.title: Decoherence
c118.detail: Zeh and others showed that interaction with the environment makes quantum superpositions invisible in everyday life. It explains part of the measurement problem but is not a full solution.
c118.lesson: It began to explain why everyday life looks classical.

c119.title: String Theory and Gravity
c119.detail: Scherk and Schwarz showed that particles including gravity arise naturally in string theory, making it a candidate for quantum gravity.
c119.lesson: A candidate linking gravity and quantum theory appeared.

c120.title: Aspect's Experiment
c120.detail: Aspect and others confirmed violation of Bell's inequality, showing entanglement is real. Nobel Prize in Physics 2022 (Aspect, Clauser, Zeilinger).
c120.lesson: The riddle of observation was tested in the lab.

c121.title: First Superstring Revolution
c121.detail: Green and Schwarz showed that superstring theory is mathematically consistent. Spacetime is taken to have ten dimensions.
c121.lesson: String theory suddenly became the leading candidate.

c122.title: Eternal Inflation
c122.detail: Vilenkin, Linde and others proposed that inflation continues in places across the universe, so countless universes can arise.
c122.lesson: Our universe may be one of many.
c122.label: About 1983–86

c123.title: M-Theory
c123.detail: Witten proposed that the five superstring theories are different aspects of an eleven-dimensional M-theory (the second superstring revolution).
c123.lesson: Separate theories connected to a single root.

c124.title: Braneworld
c124.detail: Randall, Sundrum and others proposed that our universe is a membrane (brane) floating in higher dimensions.
c124.lesson: Our universe may be merely a membrane.

c125.title: The Landscape
c125.detail: Susskind and others argued that string theory has a huge number of vacua (the landscape), each potentially a universe with different laws of physics.
c125.lesson: The laws of physics may be a chosen outcome.

c126.title: Nobel Prize for Entanglement
c126.detail: Aspect, Clauser and Zeilinger won the Nobel Prize in Physics for experiments on quantum entanglement.
c126.lesson: The measurement problem became a matter of technology too.

c127.title: Anti-Frame Theory
c127.detail: On January 9, 2026, the note account "ANTI FRAME" published the Anti-Frame Theory. It tries to add the observer's "overwhelming agency" to debates on the measurement problem and many-worlds, and later moved its activity to not/on (presented as the proposer's own theory).
c127.lesson: Do not place the observing subject outside the theory.

c128.title: Anti-Frame Theory 2.0
c128.detail: On June 15, 2026, the Anti-Frame Theory was updated to 2.0 (presented as the proposer's own theory).
c128.lesson: Theories too are re-observed and updated.

c129.title: Composition of the Universe
c129.detail: WMAP observations precisely showed the universe is about 13.8 billion years old and that ordinary matter is only about 5%.
c129.lesson: We know only 5% of the universe.

c130.title: Higgs Boson
c130.detail: The LHC discovered the Higgs boson, which gives particles mass.
c130.lesson: Confirmed about 50 years after its prediction.

c131.title: First Gravitational Waves
c131.detail: LIGO first detected gravitational waves from a black hole merger, 100 years after Einstein's prediction.
c131.lesson: The era of "listening" to the universe began.

c132.title: Imaging a Black Hole
c132.detail: The Event Horizon Telescope imaged the shadow of the black hole at the center of galaxy M87.

c133.title: The Hubble Tension
c133.detail: Attention focused on the discrepancy between measurements of the expansion rate depending on method (the Hubble tension).
c133.lesson: A discrepancy may be a doorway to new physics.

c134.title: Webb Telescope
c134.detail: The James Webb Space Telescope was launched and its first images were released in 2022. It observes galaxies close to just after the Big Bang.
c134.label: 2021 (first images 2022)

c135.title: Spread of Generative AI
c135.detail: Generative AI spread, and the ways people search for, organize and conceive knowledge began to change.

c136.title: Apophis Flyby
c136.detail: Asteroid Apophis will pass very close to Earth on April 13, 2029. No impact is predicted.
c136.lesson: The motions of space can be predicted by calculation.

c137.title: Total Eclipse in Japan
c137.detail: A total solar eclipse is predicted on September 2, 2035, visible from northern Kanto to parts of Hokuriku.
c137.lesson: The alignment of Sun, Moon and Earth is known decades ahead.

c138.title: Halley's Comet
c138.detail: Halley's Comet, with a period of about 76 years, is predicted to next approach Earth around 2061.
c138.lesson: Knowing the cycle lets us await the future.

c139.title: Voyager 1's Approach
c139.detail: Voyager 1 is estimated to pass near another star (Gliese 445) in about 40,000 years.
c139.lesson: A probe humanity sent will travel longer than humanity.
c139.label: About 40,000 years from now

c140.title: The Next Ice Age?
c140.detail: Depending on Earth's orbit, CO₂ levels and other conditions, the next ice age is thought to be tens of thousands of years away. The influence of human activity is also debated.
c140.lesson: The future climate also depends on our choices.
c140.label: About 50,000 years from now (debated)

c141.title: Will the Oceans Be Lost?
c141.detail: The Sun slowly brightens, and one prediction says Earth's oceans begin to evaporate in about a billion years.
c141.lesson: A star's lifespan is also a planet's lifespan.
c141.label: About 1 billion years from now (debated)

c142.title: Milky Way and Andromeda
c142.detail: The Milky Way and Andromeda were long expected to collide and merge in about 4.5 billion years. Recent studies put the chance at about fifty-fifty.
c142.lesson: Galaxies, too, meet or pass each other by.
c142.label: About 4.5 billion years from now (debated)

c143.title: The Sun Becomes a Red Giant
c143.detail: The Sun will use up its hydrogen, swell and become a red giant, predicted in about 5 billion years.
c143.lesson: Our star, too, has an end.
c143.label: About 5 billion years from now

c144.title: On to a White Dwarf
c144.detail: After the red giant stage, the Sun will shed its outer layers and become a small white dwarf.
c144.label: About 8 billion years from now

c145.title: Distant Galaxies Disappear
c145.detail: If the expansion keeps accelerating, surrounding galaxies recede and become unobservable.
c145.lesson: Seeing today's universe may be possible only today.
c145.label: About 100 billion years from now

c146.title: Star Birth Ends
c146.detail: Gas runs out and almost no new stars form.
c146.lesson: Even the age of stars has an end.
c146.label: From about 1 trillion years from now

c147.title: The Last Star
c147.detail: The longest-lived red dwarfs also burn out, and the age of stars is expected to end.
c147.lesson: The time with light is only a sliver of cosmic history.
c147.label: About 100 trillion years from now

c148.title: The Universe Beyond
c148.detail: The evaporation of black holes and how the universe ends (heat death, Big Crunch and so on) remain unsettled.
c148.lesson: No one yet knows what lies beyond.
c148.label: Later (debated)

c149.title: Splitting of the Forces
c149.detail: Forces thought to have been one split into gravity, the strong force, the weak force and electromagnetism. A theoretical estimate.
c149.lesson: The form of today's physical laws was set in the early universe.
c149.label: Just after birth (theory)

c150.title: Matter and Antimatter
c150.detail: Matter and antimatter were made in nearly equal amounts, but slightly more matter remained. The reason for this difference is still not fully understood.
c150.lesson: Our very existence is an unsolved problem of the universe.
c150.label: Within 1 second of birth (theory)

c151.title: Neutrino Decoupling
c151.detail: As the universe cooled, neutrinos almost stopped interacting with other matter and streamed away freely. They are thought still to fill the universe.
c151.lesson: Particles that barely touch carry the memory of the universe.
c151.label: About 1 second after birth (theory)

c152.title: Matter Era
c152.detail: The energy of matter exceeded the energy of light, making gravitational structure formation easier.
c152.lesson: From the age of light to the age of matter.
c152.label: About 50,000 years after birth

c153.title: First Supernovae and Heavy Elements
c153.detail: The first giant stars exploded, scattering heavy elements such as carbon, oxygen and iron through space.
c153.lesson: A star's death becomes the material for the next generation.
c153.label: About 13.6 billion years ago

c154.title: Growth of Giant Black Holes
c154.detail: The James Webb Space Telescope has found evidence of giant black holes already present a few hundred million years after the universe's birth. How they grew is at the research frontier.
c154.lesson: Objects that grew faster than expected pose questions to theory.
c154.label: About 13.3 billion years ago

c155.title: Galaxy Mergers
c155.detail: In its youth the Milky Way swallowed small galaxies many times. Gaia observations showed traces of a large merger (the Gaia-Sausage) about 8–11 billion years ago.
c155.label: About 9.5 billion years ago

c156.title: The Milky Way's Disk
c156.detail: The Milky Way took shape as a disk of stars, before the Sun was born.
c156.lesson: Our galaxy's form is older than the Sun.
c156.label: About 9 billion years ago

c157.title: Ignition of the Young Sun
c157.detail: Hydrogen fusion began at the center of a disk of gas and dust, and the Sun began to shine.
c157.lesson: A star is born at the moment fusion ignites.
c157.label: About 4.56 billion years ago

c158.title: Birth of Jupiter
c158.detail: Jupiter, the largest planet, grew quickly in the early solar system. Its gravity affected the orbits of other planets and the asteroid belt.
c158.lesson: A giant planet shaped the solar system.
c158.label: About 4.55 billion years ago

c159.title: Giant Impact
c159.detail: The leading theory is that a Mars-sized protoplanet struck the young Earth and the Moon formed from the debris.
c159.lesson: The Moon is a child of Earth's great accident.
c159.label: About 4.51 billion years ago

c160.title: Oldest Minerals
c160.detail: Zircon crystals found in Australia are about 4.4 billion years old, suggesting liquid water may already have existed then.
c160.lesson: A tiny crystal tells of Earth's earliest days.
c160.label: About 4.39 billion years ago

c161.title: Late Heavy Bombardment
c161.detail: There is a theory that many bodies struck the Moon and Earth about 4.1–3.8 billion years ago. Its duration and scale are still debated.
c161.lesson: Weigh the strength of a theory apart from the strength of evidence.
c161.label: About 4.1–3.8 billion years ago (debated)

c162.title: Stromatolites
c162.detail: Layered rocks made by microbes such as cyanobacteria. Examples about 3.5 billion years old have been found in Western Australia.
c162.lesson: The oldest life left its shape in rock.
c162.label: About 3.5 billion years ago

c163.title: First Snowball Earth
c163.detail: Rising oxygen reduced greenhouse methane, and the entire Earth may have been covered in ice (the Huronian glaciation).
c163.lesson: Life changed the environment, and the environment tested life.
c163.label: About 2.3 billion years ago

c164.title: Oldest Multicellular Algae
c164.detail: Fossils of multicellular organisms resembling red algae have been found in Canada. An early example of cells dividing roles.
c164.label: About 1.2 billion years ago

c165.title: Supercontinent Rodinia
c165.detail: The continents gathered into one supercontinent. Its later breakup is thought to have influenced snowball glaciations and the evolution of life.
c165.lesson: The movement of continents shakes climate and life.
c165.label: About 1.1 billion years ago

c166.title: Earliest Animals
c166.detail: Animals with sponge-like bodies are thought to have appeared. There is molecular-clock and chemical-fossil evidence, but confirmation as fossils is still debated.
c166.lesson: The origin of animals is still being explored.
c166.label: About 600 million years ago (debated)

c167.title: Oldest Vertebrates
c167.detail: Small fish-like creatures such as Myllokunmingia have been found in China's Chengjiang fauna.
c167.lesson: Our distant ancestor was a small fish.
c167.label: About 520 million years ago

c168.title: Burgess Shale
c168.detail: A fossil bed in Canada preserves the diverse Cambrian animals in fine detail, known for strange creatures such as Opabinia.
c168.lesson: Strange animals show evolution's trial and error.
c168.label: About 510 million years ago

c169.title: End-Ordovician Mass Extinction
c169.detail: Glaciation and falling sea levels are thought to have wiped out about 85% of marine species (the first of the Big Five).
c169.lesson: Climate change is the greatest threat to life.
c169.label: About 445 million years ago

c170.title: Tiktaalik
c170.detail: A fossil with traits between fish and four-legged animals. It has a neck, and its fins contain bones leading to fingers. Discovered in Canada in 2004.
c170.lesson: A midpoint in evolution was left in a fossil.
c170.label: About 380 million years ago

c171.title: Seed Plants Appear
c171.detail: Seed plants, able to reproduce even on dry land, appeared. They would form the later forests.
c171.lesson: The invention of the seed spread plants into every corner of the land.
c171.label: About 360 million years ago

c172.title: First Reptiles
c172.detail: Animals that lay eggs on land appeared, making life away from water possible.
c172.lesson: The dry-shelled egg completed life on land.
c172.label: About 310 million years ago

c173.title: Supercontinent Pangaea
c173.detail: All the continents gathered into one. Vast interiors were dry and the climate was extreme.
c173.lesson: Continents that gather will part again.
c173.label: About 290 million years ago

c174.title: Reptiles Return to the Sea
c174.detail: Reptiles such as ichthyosaurs returned to the sea and took on dolphin-like forms.
c174.lesson: Evolution can also go back to where it started.
c174.label: About 250 million years ago

c175.title: End-Triassic Mass Extinction
c175.detail: Huge volcanic activity and other causes wiped out many species. The surviving dinosaurs flourished in the Jurassic.
c175.lesson: One's extinction is another's chance to leap.
c175.label: About 201 million years ago

c176.title: Giant Sauropods
c176.detail: Giant long-necked herbivorous dinosaurs such as Brachiosaurus flourished, becoming among the largest land animals.
c176.lesson: Gigantism was supported by abundant plants.
c176.label: About 160 million years ago

c177.title: Feathered Dinosaurs
c177.detail: Many dinosaur fossils with traces of feathers have been found in China, supporting the evolution of birds from dinosaurs.
c177.label: About 120 million years ago

c178.title: Tyrannosaurus
c178.detail: A large carnivorous dinosaur that lived near the end of the dinosaur age. The largest individuals reached about 12 m.
c178.lesson: Even the apex predator was helpless before an asteroid.
c178.label: About 68 million years ago

c179.title: Chicxulub Impact
c179.detail: An asteroid about 10 km across struck Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, drastically changing Earth's environment.
c179.lesson: A single body rewrote the history of life.
c179.label: About 66 million years ago

c180.title: Paleocene–Eocene Warming
c180.detail: Earth's temperature is thought to have risen about 5–8 °C in a short time. Large amounts of carbon are believed to have been released, and it is used for comparison with modern warming.
c180.lesson: Read the present from past abrupt changes.
c180.label: About 56 million years ago (PETM)

c181.title: Ancestors of Whales
c181.detail: From small land mammals, through species living by the water, evolution toward whales proceeded. Fossils such as Pakicetus and Ambulocetus are known.
c181.lesson: From land to sea. Evolution can change course greatly.
c181.label: About 48 million years ago

c182.title: Sahelanthropus
c182.detail: A skull about 7 million years old found in Chad, central Africa. Considered a candidate for the oldest human.
c182.lesson: The origin of humans is still shrouded in mist.
c182.label: About 6.9 million years ago

c183.title: Orrorin
c183.detail: A fossil about 6 million years old found in Kenya. The shape of its femur suggests it may have walked on two legs.
c183.lesson: The origin of bipedalism may be older than thought.
c183.label: About 6 million years ago

c184.title: Laetoli Footprints
c184.detail: In Tanzania, bipedal footprints remain on volcanic ash about 3.66 million years old.
c184.lesson: Volcanic ash copied our ancestors' steps.
c184.label: About 3.66 million years ago

c185.title: Oldest Genus Homo
c185.detail: A jawbone about 2.8 million years old found in Ethiopia is considered the oldest example of the genus Homo.
c185.lesson: The boundary of "human" shifts bit by bit.
c185.label: About 2.8 million years ago

c186.title: Dmanisi Hominins
c186.detail: Fossils about 1.8 million years old found in Georgia. Among the oldest humans to leave Africa. They traveled far even with small brains.
c186.lesson: Brain size alone did not decide the journey.
c186.label: About 1.8 million years ago

c187.title: Hand Axe
c187.detail: A stone tool shaped symmetrically. Emblematic of the Acheulean culture, made in nearly the same form over a long period.
c187.lesson: The sense of shaping something beautifully is very old.
c187.label: About 1.7 million years ago

c188.title: Chibanian
c188.detail: A record of Earth's magnetic reversal remains in strata in Ichihara, Chiba Prefecture. That age was named "Chibanian" (Chiba age).
c188.lesson: Strata in Japan gave their name to a geological age.
c188.label: About 770,000 years ago (magnetic reversal)

c189.title: Peking Man
c189.detail: Homo erectus fossils found at Zhoukoudian near Beijing. Traces of life about 700,000–400,000 years ago; evidence of fire use has also been debated.
c189.lesson: Traces of life around a fire remain in the cave.
c189.label: About 700,000–400,000 years ago

c190.title: Mitochondrial Eve
c190.detail: Tracing modern humans' mitochondrial DNA leads to a woman in Africa about 150,000–200,000 years ago. Not the first human, but a common maternal ancestor.
c190.lesson: Tracing genes back, we meet humanity's common ancestor.
c190.label: About 150,000–200,000 years ago

c191.title: People Who Ate from the Sea
c191.detail: In a cave at Pinnacle Point, South Africa, traces of shellfish eating and pigment use about 160,000 years ago have been found.
c191.lesson: Coastal life may have helped humans survive.
c191.label: About 164,000 years ago

c192.title: Blombos Cave Engravings
c192.detail: In a South African cave, patterns engraved on red ochre about 73,000 years old have been found. An early example of symbolic thought.
c192.lesson: The mind that engraves meaning may have begun here.
c192.label: About 73,000 years ago

c193.title: Toba Supereruption
c193.detail: A supereruption occurred at Toba in Indonesia. Some argue the human population shrank, but the extent of its effect is debated.
c193.lesson: The impact of huge eruptions is still disputed.
c193.label: About 74,000 years ago

c194.title: Crossing the Sea to Australia
c194.detail: Humans crossed the sea and reached the Australian continent. Sites about 65,000 years old are known.
c194.lesson: Crossing the sea required boats and planning.
c194.label: About 65,000 years ago

c195.title: Venus of Hohle Fels
c195.detail: A female figure carved from mammoth ivory, about 40,000 years old, was found in a cave in Germany. Among the oldest figurative sculptures.
c195.lesson: People carved forms to convey their thoughts.
c195.label: About 40,000 years ago

c196.title: Chauvet Cave
c196.detail: A cave in France holds vivid animal paintings about 36,000 years old.
c196.lesson: The earliest pictures already showed great skill.
c196.label: About 36,000 years ago

c197.title: Venus Figurines
c197.detail: Small figurines of full-figured women were made across Europe, including some of the oldest fired-clay statues.
c197.lesson: The technique of hardening by firing began with art.
c197.label: About 27,000 years ago

c198.title: Lascaux Cave
c198.detail: The paintings of Lascaux Cave in France are said to have been made about 17,000 years ago. Hundreds of animals leap across the walls.
c198.lesson: The cave was a prehistoric museum.
c198.label: About 17,000 years ago

c199.title: Oldest Pottery
c199.detail: Pottery fragments about 16,000 years old have been found at the Odai Yamamoto I site in Aomori. Among the oldest in the world.
c199.lesson: Pottery was invented early in the Japanese archipelago too.
c199.label: About 16,500 years ago

c200.title: Life with Dogs
c200.detail: Dogs, split from wolves, began living beside humans. The timing is debated, with some theories going back 30,000 years.
c200.lesson: The first domestic animal was a friend.
c200.label: About 14,000 years ago (debated)

c201.title: Natufian Culture
c201.detail: The Natufians of western Asia lived nearly settled lives before farming, gathering and storing wild grain.
c201.label: About 12,500 years ago

c202.title: Dawn of Rice Farming
c202.detail: Rice cultivation began in the Yangtze basin. Rice farming later spread to East and Southeast Asia.
c202.lesson: Rice supported Asian life and population.

c203.title: Çatalhöyük
c203.detail: A large Neolithic settlement in what is now Turkey. Houses were entered from the roof, and wall paintings were made.

c204.title: Use of Copper
c204.detail: The technique of smelting and using copper spread. It eventually led to the Bronze and Iron Ages.
c204.lesson: The fire that melts metal changed the age of tools.

c205.title: Nabta Playa
c205.detail: In the desert of southern Egypt are stone alignments. Some suggest a link to celestial bodies, but the interpretation is not settled.
c205.lesson: Whether it was the oldest observatory is still unknown.
c205.label: About 7,000 years ago

c206.title: Invention of the Wheel
c206.detail: Wheeled vehicles appeared across wide regions from around 3500 BCE.
c206.lesson: A rotating wheel changed the power to carry.

c207.title: Stonehenge
c207.detail: A huge stone circle in England. The first earthen ring is dated to around 3000 BCE and the stone arrangement to around 2500 BCE. A link to the solstices has been suggested.
c207.lesson: The Sun's motion was copied into an arrangement of stones.

c208.title: Venus Tablet
c208.detail: A Babylonian clay tablet records the cycle of Venus's appearances. An early example of systematic observation of celestial cycles.
c208.lesson: Keep recording and the rules of the heavens appear.

c209.title: Eclipse Records in Oracle Bones
c209.detail: Shang oracle bone inscriptions record solar and lunar eclipses.

c210.title: Thales' Eclipse Prediction
c210.detail: Herodotus reports that Thales of Miletus predicted a solar eclipse. The actual method and accuracy are unknown.
c210.lesson: He tried to see a phenomenon thought divine as a natural regularity.

c211.title: Metonic Cycle
c211.detail: Meton of Athens showed that solar and lunar calendars nearly coincide every 19 years. It became the basis of later calendars.
c211.lesson: The gap between Sun and Moon was matched with numbers.

c212.title: Discovery of Precession
c212.detail: Hipparchus is said to have found, by comparing star catalogs, that the equinox point shifts slowly. It completes a cycle in about 26,000 years.
c212.lesson: Compare old records and slow motions become visible.

c213.title: Antikythera Mechanism
c213.detail: A bronze gear device found in a Greek shipwreck. Thought to have calculated the positions of the Sun and Moon, eclipse cycles and more.
c213.lesson: Precision machinery existed even in antiquity.
c213.label: 2nd–1st century BCE

c214.title: Julian Calendar
c214.detail: Caesar established a calendar of 365 days with a leap year every four years. It was used for nearly 1,600 years.
c214.lesson: Calendar reform was also a political task.

c215.title: Zhang Heng's Seismoscope
c215.detail: Zhang Heng of the Later Han is said to have built a device indicating the direction of earthquakes. Also known for his armillary sphere and astronomical writings.
c215.lesson: Earthquakes and stars were observed by the same scholar.

c216.title: Oldest Supernova Record
c216.detail: Later Han records note a "guest star" visible for about eight months. Thought to correspond to a present supernova remnant (SN 185).
c216.lesson: Old records connect with modern astronomy.

c217.title: Aryabhata
c217.detail: In the Aryabhatiya, India's Aryabhata discussed Earth's rotation and the mechanism of solar and lunar eclipses.
c217.lesson: Astronomy developed deeply in India too.

c218.title: Birth of Algebra
c218.detail: Al-Khwarizmi of Baghdad wrote Al-Jabr and systematized the solving of equations. His name gave rise to "algorithm."
c218.lesson: Organizing mathematics became a tool for astronomical calculation.

c219.title: Book of Fixed Stars
c219.detail: The Persian astronomer al-Sufi wrote the Book of Fixed Stars and gave one of the earliest records of the Andromeda Galaxy.
c219.lesson: They had already recorded a galaxy visible to the naked eye.

c220.title: SN 1006
c220.detail: Recorded around the world as the brightest supernova in history. Said to have shone in the night sky with about a quarter of the Moon's brightness.
c220.lesson: Records from several countries support a single explosion.

c221.title: Book of Optics
c221.detail: Ibn al-Haytham argued that we see objects by light entering the eye and investigated the nature of light by experiment.
c221.lesson: The idea of confirming by experiment shaped the method of science.

c222.title: Shen Kuo's Dream Pool Essays
c222.detail: Shen Kuo of the Song described that a compass needle deviates from true north (magnetic declination) and calendar reform.
c222.lesson: An encyclopedia of carefully recorded observations.

c223.title: Maragheh Observatory
c223.detail: An observatory with large instruments was built at Maragheh in Persia, led by Nasir al-Din al-Tusi.

c224.title: Shoushi Calendar
c224.detail: Guo Shoujing and others of the Yuan completed the Shoushi calendar based on observation, determining the length of the year precisely. It later influenced Japan's Jōkyō calendar.

c225.title: Ulugh Beg's Star Catalog
c225.detail: At the Samarkand observatory, positions of about 1,000 stars were measured precisely. The finest star catalog before the telescope.
c225.lesson: With well-devised instruments, the naked eye can measure precisely.

c226.title: Tycho's Supernova
c226.detail: Tycho Brahe observed a new star in Cassiopeia, casting doubt on the idea that the heavens are unchanging.
c226.lesson: The common sense that the heavens never change collapsed.

c227.title: Execution of Bruno
c227.detail: Giordano Bruno argued the universe is infinite and the stars are bodies like the Sun, and was executed as a heretic. Theological claims were also among the grounds.
c227.lesson: Differences in views of the universe sometimes became fights over life.

c228.title: Kepler's Supernova
c228.detail: The last supernova visible to the naked eye within the Milky Way (SN 1604). Observed by Kepler and Galileo.
c228.lesson: The last Milky Way supernova observed by the naked eye.

c229.title: Trial of Galileo
c229.detail: Galileo was summoned before the Roman Inquisition for supporting heliocentrism. Thereafter he continued his research under house arrest.
c229.lesson: An example of truth pressed down by authority.

c230.title: Discovery of Titan
c230.detail: Huygens discovered Saturn's moon Titan and later clarified the shape of Saturn's rings.
c230.lesson: The telescope kept revealing new worlds.

c231.title: Newton's Miracle Year
c231.detail: While the university was closed for the plague, Newton is said to have advanced calculus, the analysis of light and the idea of gravity (1665–66).

c232.title: Finite Speed of Light
c232.detail: Rømer showed that the speed of light is finite from the timing shifts of eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io.
c232.lesson: The speed of light was measured from a cosmic phenomenon.

c233.title: Halley's Comet Prediction
c233.detail: From past records, Halley predicted that the comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682 were the same body returning on a cycle of about 76 years. It reappeared in 1758.
c233.lesson: When a prediction came true, science gained trust.
c233.label: 1705 (prediction)

c234.title: Discovery of Uranus
c234.detail: William Herschel discovered a new planet with a telescope. The first planet found beyond those known since antiquity.
c234.lesson: The sky was still full of new discoveries.

c235.title: First Asteroid, Ceres
c235.detail: Piazzi discovered a small body between Mars and Jupiter. Later classified as a dwarf planet.
c235.lesson: Even between planets there were small worlds.

c236.title: Fraunhofer Lines
c236.detail: Fraunhofer recorded that sunlight split by a prism has many dark lines. They were later used to analyze composition.
c236.lesson: Dark lines in light tell the makeup of stars.

c237.title: Measuring Stellar Parallax
c237.detail: Bessel first measured the distance to 61 Cygni. The distance to a star was measured directly for the first time.
c237.lesson: A cosmic yardstick was first obtained.

c238.title: Doppler Effect
c238.detail: Doppler theorized that wavelength changes when a source of sound or light moves. It was later used to measure stellar motion and cosmic expansion.
c238.lesson: Changes in color reveal a body's motion.

c239.title: Spectroscopy
c239.detail: Kirchhoff and Bunsen confirmed from dark lines in sunlight that the Sun contains iron and sodium.
c239.lesson: The makeup of unreachable stars was learned from light.

c240.title: Michelson–Morley Experiment
c240.detail: Seeking to confirm the "ether," the medium carrying light, they looked for differences in the speed of light due to Earth's motion, but found none.
c240.lesson: A failed experiment opened the way to relativity.

c241.title: Discovery of Radioactivity
c241.detail: Becquerel found radiation emitted by uranium compounds. It later became a clue for measuring the age of stars and Earth.
c241.lesson: Unseen radiation became a yardstick of time.

c242.title: Discovery of the Atomic Nucleus
c242.detail: Rutherford's experiment showed a small, heavy nucleus at the center of the atom.
c242.lesson: The atom was almost entirely empty.

c243.title: Period–Luminosity Relation
c243.detail: Henrietta Leavitt found a relation between the brightness and period of variable stars. It became the basis of Hubble's and others' distance measurements.
c243.lesson: A star's flicker became a cosmic yardstick.

c244.title: Discovery of Cosmic Rays
c244.detail: Hess ascended by balloon and confirmed that radiation was stronger aloft than on the ground, discovering particles from space.
c244.lesson: High in the sky, he met particles from the cosmos.

c245.title: Schwarzschild Solution
c245.detail: An exact solution of the equations of general relativity was obtained soon after. It later led to the theory of black holes.
c245.lesson: A strange object lurked in the solution of an equation.

c246.title: Cosmological Constant
c246.detail: Einstein added a cosmological constant to his equations to keep the universe static. He later thought it unnecessary, but it drew renewed attention as a candidate for dark energy.
c246.lesson: A discarded term revived 100 years later.

c247.title: Friedmann Equations
c247.detail: Friedmann derived solutions in which the universe expands or contracts. They became the basic equations of modern cosmology.
c247.lesson: The mathematics showed a non-static universe first.

c248.title: Discovery of Pluto
c248.detail: Pluto was discovered from photographs taken by Tombaugh. In 2006 it was reclassified as a dwarf planet.
c248.lesson: The definition of a planet is revised by discovery.

c249.title: Chandrasekhar Limit
c249.detail: Chandrasekhar calculated the upper mass limit a white dwarf can support (about 1.4 solar masses). Stars beyond it head toward supernovae or black holes.
c249.lesson: A star's final fate is decided by mass.

c250.title: Discovery of Cosmic Radio Waves
c250.detail: Jansky received radio waves from the direction of the Milky Way, and radio astronomy was born.
c250.lesson: The age of seeing the universe by unseen light began.

c251.title: Source of Stellar Energy
c251.detail: Bethe showed theoretically that nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium is the energy source of stars.
c251.lesson: The mechanism by which stars shine was finally understood.

c252.title: Miller's Experiment
c252.detail: Miller discharged electricity in an apparatus modeling the early Earth's atmosphere and confirmed that amino acids formed.
c252.lesson: The ingredients of life may form naturally.

c253.title: Origin of the Elements
c253.detail: The B²FH paper systematically showed how elements are made inside stars and in supernova explosions.
c253.lesson: The elements of our bodies were made by stars.

c254.title: Van Allen Belts
c254.detail: The probe Explorer 1 discovered the radiation belts surrounding Earth.
c254.lesson: Going into space revealed unseen belts enveloping Earth.

c255.title: First X-ray Source
c255.detail: Rocket observations discovered Scorpius X-1. X-ray astronomy has expanded since.
c255.lesson: New objects were found by unseen light.

c256.title: Discovery of Quasars
c256.detail: Objects that look like stars yet emit enormous energy from great distances were found. Thought to be the centers of active galaxies where giant black holes swallow matter.
c256.lesson: Far out in the universe were astonishing objects.

c257.title: Discovery of Pulsars
c257.detail: Jocelyn Bell and others discovered an object emitting radio waves at regular intervals. It proved to be a rotating neutron star.
c257.lesson: At first the regular signal was suspected to be alien communication.

c258.title: Cygnus X-1
c258.detail: One member of an X-ray emitting binary was found to be an invisible heavy object, making it a leading black hole candidate.
c258.lesson: An invisible body was found from the motion around it.

c259.title: Voyager Launches
c259.detail: Voyager 1 and 2 were launched to explore the outer planets. They carry the Golden Record and still fly beyond the solar system.
c259.lesson: Carrying humanity's letter, they continue their journey in the sea of stars.

c260.title: Asteroid Impact Hypothesis
c260.detail: The Alvarezes, father and son, proposed from an iridium anomaly in strata that an asteroid impact caused the extinction of the dinosaurs. The Chicxulub crater was later found.
c260.lesson: A thin layer in the strata solved the riddle of extinction.

c261.title: Supernova 1987A
c261.detail: A supernova exploded in the Large Magellanic Cloud, and Japan's Kamiokande caught its neutrinos. Masatoshi Koshiba won the Nobel Prize in 2002.
c261.lesson: Neutrinos from space were detected for the first time.

c262.title: COBE Satellite
c262.detail: A satellite to measure the cosmic background radiation precisely was launched. In 1992 it found tiny fluctuations in temperature.
c262.lesson: A baby picture of the universe was taken.

c263.title: Comet Strikes Jupiter
c263.detail: Comet Shoemaker–Levy 9 broke apart and its collision with Jupiter was observed. Awareness spread that bodies can strike Earth too.
c263.lesson: Witnessing another planet's impacts made us think about preparing Earth.

c264.title: Hubble Deep Field
c264.detail: The Hubble telescope imaged one tiny patch of sky for a long time and captured thousands of galaxies.
c264.lesson: A dark speck of sky was packed with galaxies.

c265.title: WMAP Satellite
c265.detail: It observed the cosmic background radiation precisely and determined the age and composition of the universe with high accuracy.
c265.lesson: The universe's age was found to be 13.8 billion years.

c266.title: Cassini at Saturn
c266.detail: The probe arrived at Saturn, and in 2005 the small probe Huygens landed on Titan. Over 13 years it revealed the rings and moons.
c266.lesson: Saturn and its moons raised the possibility of life.

c267.title: Definition of Planet and Pluto
c267.detail: The International Astronomical Union defined "planet" and classified Pluto as a dwarf planet.
c267.lesson: Classifications are updated to fit new discoveries.

c268.title: Large Hadron Collider
c268.detail: A 27-km-circumference accelerator began operating on the Swiss–French border. It led to the discovery of the Higgs boson in 2012.
c268.lesson: A giant instrument for examining the smallest things.

c269.title: Hayabusa Returns
c269.detail: It brought back samples of asteroid Itokawa. Its return after a seven-year journey was the world's first sample return from an asteroid.
c269.lesson: A probe that overcame failures came home.

c270.title: Rosetta's Comet Landing
c270.detail: Philae, the lander of Europe's Rosetta probe, landed on a comet for the first time.
c270.lesson: We touched an ancient fossil of the solar system.

c271.title: Proxima Centauri b
c271.detail: A planet about the size of Earth was found around the star nearest the Sun.
c271.lesson: The neighboring star has a planet too.

c272.title: TRAPPIST-1
c272.detail: Seven Earth-sized planets were found around a star about 40 light-years away. Several are in the habitable zone.
c272.lesson: Several Earth-sized worlds around a single star.

c273.title: Parker Solar Probe
c273.detail: A probe that plunges into the Sun's corona. It came closer to the Sun than any human-made object in history.
c273.lesson: A probe entered the Sun's atmosphere.

c274.title: Hayabusa2 Sample Return
c274.detail: Samples from asteroid Ryugu reached Earth. Organic matter and amino acids were found, showing that the ingredients of life exist in space.
c274.lesson: The ingredients of life may have come from space.

c275.title: DART Mission
c275.detail: A probe was crashed into asteroid Dimorphos and successfully changed its orbit. Humanity changed a celestial body's orbit for the first time.
c275.lesson: Technology to protect Earth from impacts was tested.

c276.title: Gravitational-Wave Background
c276.detail: Pulsar timing arrays showed evidence of low-frequency gravitational waves spread across the whole universe. Thought to originate from supermassive black hole binaries and the like.
c276.lesson: The universe is constantly shaking with gravitational waves.

c277.title: Vega Becomes the Pole Star
c277.detail: Because of precession, in about 13,700 years Vega in Lyra will be near the position of the north pole star.
c277.lesson: The pole star is not eternal.

c278.title: Betelgeuse Goes Supernova
c278.detail: The red supergiant Betelgeuse will someday explode as a supernova. The timing is said to be within the next 100,000 years but is uncertain. It is far enough to pose no danger to Earth.
c278.lesson: Someday a star visible even in daytime will appear.

c279.title: Gliese 710's Approach
c279.detail: The star Gliese 710 will pass within about 0.1 light-year of the solar system in about 1.3 million years. It could disturb the Oort cloud and increase comets.

c280.title: A New Supercontinent
c280.detail: Predictions say continental drift will create a new supercontinent in about 250 million years. Its shape varies by study.

c281.title: Electroweak Separation
c281.detail: Electromagnetism and the weak force separated. Particles are thought to have acquired mass at this time. A theoretical estimate.
c281.label: About a trillionth of a second after birth (theory)

c282.title: Quark Confinement
c282.detail: The universe cooled and quarks bound together into protons and neutrons.
c282.label: About a millionth of a second after birth (theory)

c283.title: Reheating
c283.detail: Inflation ended and its energy turned to heat, making the universe hot. A theoretical estimate.
c283.label: Just after birth (theory)

c284.title: Baryogenesis
c284.detail: Matter slightly exceeding antimatter remained and became the material of today's stars and galaxies.
c284.label: Within 1 second of birth

c285.title: Electron–Positron Annihilation
c285.detail: Electrons and positrons collided and turned into light. Only the slightly more numerous electrons remained.
c285.label: A few seconds after birth

c286.title: Radiation Era
c286.detail: The era when most of the universe's energy was light (radiation). Light ruled over matter.
c286.label: Until tens of thousands of years after birth

c287.title: Matter Clumps by Gravity
c287.detail: Dark matter formed density variations first, later seeding the formation of stars and galaxies.
c287.label: About 30,000 years after birth

c288.title: Sound Ripples
c288.detail: Sound-like waves traveled through the plasma where light and matter were mixed. Traces of the waves remain today in the distribution of galaxies.
c288.label: Until about 380,000 years after birth

c289.title: Birth of Hydrogen Atoms
c289.detail: Electrons joined protons to form hydrogen atoms, and light could travel far.
c289.label: About 380,000 years after birth

c290.title: The Background Radiation Afterward
c290.detail: The light of recombination filled the universe as it cooled and is now observed as microwaves.
c290.label: After about 380,000 years

c291.title: Before Cosmic Dawn
c291.detail: There were no stars yet and neutral hydrogen gas spread through the universe. Research probing it with 21 cm radio waves is advancing.
c291.label: About 13.78 billion years ago

c292.title: Dark Matter Halos
c292.detail: Clumps of dark matter grew, and their gravity drew in hydrogen gas.
c292.label: About 13.7 billion years ago

c293.title: Population III Stars
c293.detail: Giant stars made of only hydrogen and helium. Theoretical objects not yet directly observed.
c293.label: About 13.65 billion years ago

c294.title: Seeds of Black Holes
c294.detail: Seeds of supermassive black holes are thought to have formed by the collapse of the first stars or by direct collapse of gas clouds.
c294.label: About 13.55 billion years ago

c295.title: Earliest Galaxies Seen by JWST
c295.detail: The Webb telescope observed galaxies about 300 million years after birth. Some were brighter and larger than expected.
c295.label: About 13.5 billion years ago

c296.title: Merging of Protogalaxies
c296.detail: Small galaxies attracted each other by gravity and merged, growing into larger galaxies.
c296.label: About 13.3 billion years ago

c297.title: Reionization Completes
c297.detail: Ultraviolet light ionized the universe's hydrogen gas, and the universe became transparent again.
c297.label: About 12.9 billion years ago

c298.title: Globular Clusters
c298.detail: Gatherings of up to a million old stars surrounding the Milky Way. Fossil-like relics born in the young universe.
c298.label: About 12.5 billion years ago

c299.title: Age of Quasars
c299.detail: Supermassive black holes at the centers of galaxies shone brightly as they swallowed gas.
c299.label: About 12 billion years ago

c300.title: Formation of Galaxy Clusters
c300.detail: Gravity gathered galaxies, and clusters containing hundreds to thousands of galaxies began to form.
c300.label: About 11.5 billion years ago

c301.title: The Milky Way's Great Merger
c301.detail: Gaia satellite observations revealed a collision with a large galaxy, called the Gaia–Enceladus merger.
c301.label: About 10 billion years ago

c302.title: Neutron Star Mergers and Gold
c302.detail: Collisions of neutron stars make heavy elements such as gold and platinum. Gold on Earth is a fragment of these.
c302.label: About 9 billion years ago

c303.title: The Milky Way's Bar
c303.detail: A structure of stars lined up like a bar is thought to have formed in the galactic center.
c303.label: About 8 billion years ago

c304.title: Dark Energy Dominates
c304.detail: Matter's density thinned, and dark energy began to govern the universe's expansion.
c304.label: About 7 billion years ago

c305.title: Laniakea Supercluster
c305.detail: A gathering of over 100,000 galaxies including the Milky Way, connected by flows of gravity.
c305.label: About 6 billion years ago

c306.title: Molecular Cloud for the Sun
c306.detail: In an arm of the Milky Way, a cloud of gas and dust began to contract under gravity.
c306.label: About 5 billion years ago

c307.title: Oldest Solids, CAIs
c307.detail: Small white grains remaining in meteorites. Said to be the first things to solidify in the solar system and used as the age standard.
c307.label: About 4.57 billion years ago

c308.title: Chondrules
c308.detail: Small round grains in meteorites, melted at high temperature and then solidified. They convey the early solar system.
c308.label: About 4.56 billion years ago

c309.title: Formation of Planetesimals
c309.detail: Dust gathered to make small bodies, which merged further to become the seeds of planets.
c309.label: About 4.56 billion years ago

c310.title: Saturn, Uranus and Neptune
c310.detail: Following Jupiter, the other giant planets formed.
c310.label: About 4.55 billion years ago

c311.title: Formation of Mars
c311.detail: A planet much smaller than Earth, formed early in the solar system.
c311.label: About 4.54 billion years ago

c312.title: Magma Ocean
c312.detail: From the energy of impacts, the whole Earth was molten. It later cooled and a crust formed.
c312.label: About 4.45 billion years ago

c313.title: The First Crust
c313.detail: Zircon minerals show that a solid crust and water existed at this time.
c313.label: About 4.4 billion years ago

c314.title: South Pole–Aitken Basin
c314.detail: One of the solar system's largest impact basins, on the far side of the Moon. Exploration to study the Moon's interior is advancing.
c314.label: About 4.3 billion years ago

c315.title: Migration of Giant Planets
c315.detail: One theory holds that the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn migrated and rearranged the solar system's bodies.
c315.label: About 4.1 billion years ago

c316.title: Early Earth's Atmosphere
c316.detail: Carbon dioxide and water vapor released from volcanoes became the origin of Earth's atmosphere.
c316.label: About 4 billion years ago

c317.title: Chemical Traces of Life
c317.detail: Carbon traces indicating biological activity have been found in ancient rocks such as those in Greenland.
c317.label: About 3.95 billion years ago

c318.title: Isua Formations
c318.detail: Ancient strata in Greenland retain structures that may have been made by microbes.
c318.label: About 3.7 billion years ago

c319.title: Oldest Microfossils
c319.detail: Bacteria-like microfossils remain in rocks in Australia. Their authenticity is debated.
c319.label: About 3.4 billion years ago

c320.title: Nitrogen Fixation
c320.detail: Bacteria acquired the ability to take in nitrogen from the air, leading to a supply of ammonia usable by life.
c320.label: About 3.2 billion years ago

c321.title: Pongola Glaciation
c321.detail: Traces of one of the oldest ice ages exist in South Africa.
c321.label: About 2.9 billion years ago

c322.title: Gabon Biota
c322.detail: Fossils possibly of multicellular organisms were found in strata in Gabon.
c322.label: About 2.1 billion years ago

c323.title: Natural Nuclear Reactor
c323.detail: At Oklo in Gabon, a natural uranium deposit sustained a chain reaction.
c323.label: About 2 billion years ago
